objective: By the end of the lesson, learners will be better able to identify and correct sentence fragments (missing subjects and missing verbs) in the context of describing friendships and personal relationships.
materials: - Introduction to Academic Writing (3rd ed.), Chapter 1: Paragraph Format, pp14-15

stages.stage_aim: To activate interest in describing friendships and raise awareness that some English sentences feel incomplete.
stages.procedure:
- Display an image of two friends on the IWB. Elicit discussion: "Who is your best friend? What makes a good friend?" Collect 3-4 responses. 3 min.
- Present 3 fragment sentences about friendship on the IWB: Is very kind and generous. / My friend always there for me. / Usually meet at the weekend. Ask pairs: "What is wrong with these sentences? Can you fix them?" Elicit ideas but do not teach the rules yet. 3 min.
- Bridge to the lesson: "Today we will learn why these are wrong and how to fix them. In English, every sentence must have two things — let's find out what they are." 2 min.

stages.stage_aim: To diagnose how well learners can distinguish complete sentences from fragments and correct fragments by supplying missing subjects or verbs.
stages.procedure:
- Display a bespoke 6-item diagnostic quiz on the IWB. Learners see 6 sentences about friendship on screen. Three items are complete sentences; three are fragments (two missing the subject, one missing the verb).
- Students work individually in their notebooks: mark each item ✓ (complete sentence) or ✗ (fragment), then correct each fragment by adding a subject or a verb.
- Monitor closely. Note which error type (missing subject vs missing verb) causes more difficulty. Do not reveal answers yet.

stages.stage_aim: To draw out the rule that every English sentence must have a subject and a verb, and to teach two fix strategies for correcting fragments.
stages.procedure:
- Return to the diagnostic test. Use show of hands to check which items the class found hardest. Elicit corrections for the fragment items on the IWB.
- Ask: "What must every English sentence have?" Draw out the answer: a subject and a verb.
- Present the two fragment types with examples from the test:
  1. Missing subject — e.g., Is very kind and generous. → Fix: add a subject. She is very kind and generous.
  2. Missing verb — e.g., My friend always there for me. → Fix: add a verb. My friend is always there for me.
- Board the rule with both examples. Students copy into notebooks.
- Briefly note the exception: commands (e.g., Stop!) have an implied subject (you) and are not fragments.

stages.stage_aim: To apply fragment identification and correction strategies in controlled sentence-level exercises and extended paragraph-level editing, using textbook Practice 4.
stages.procedure:
- Part A: Textbook Practice 4, Part A, pp14–15 — “Step 1 Read each sentence and decide if it is a complete sentence or a fragment. Mark the fragments with an X to show that it is incorrect. Step 2 Decide what is wrong with each fragment. Is the verb missing? Is the subject missing? Step 3 Correct each fragment by adding a subject or a verb.” Students complete the 7 items individually. Pair check. Whole-class feedback using the answer key on the IWB. 7 min.
- Part B: Textbook Practice 4, Part B — Editing Practice, p15 — “Find and underline five fragments in the following paragraph. Then correct each one.” Students find and correct the 5 fragments in the My Best Friend paragraph. Pairs compare corrections. Reveal answers using the answer key on the IWB. 7 min.

stages.stage_aim: To consolidate the fragment correction rule and confirm that learners can produce complete sentences independently.
stages.procedure:
- Quick oral drill: teacher says a fragment aloud (e.g., Always listens to me.), students chorally supply the missing element (She always listens to me.). Repeat with 3–4 fragments mixing missing-subject and missing-verb types. 2 min.
- Learners write 2 complete sentences about their own best friend. Partners swap and check each other’s sentences for fragments. 3 min.
- Recap: “What must every English sentence have?” → a subject and a verb. Answer any remaining questions. 1 min.
